summary: A Healthline article explaining why people see halos (bright circles or rings) around lights, most often at night or in dim rooms. It explains that halos are caused by diffraction of light entering the eye and can be a normal response to bright light, but may signal eye disorders such as cataracts, glaucoma, Fuchs' dystrophy, keratoconus, photokeratitis, or ocular migraine, or be a side effect of LASIK, cataract surgery, or corrective lenses. It covers treatments, prevention tips, and when to see an eye doctor, noting that sudden halos with pain or blurred vision warrant prompt care.
one_line: Explains why halos appear around lights, the eye conditions and surgeries that can cause them, and when to see an eye doctor.
key_facts: Halos around lights are bright circles or rings around a light source, most often noticed at nighttime or in a dimly lit room.
Halos around lights are caused by diffraction, or bending of the light entering the eye.
Cataracts are a cloudy area that forms in the lens of the eye and are common in older people.
Fuchs' dystrophy causes the cornea to swell and is usually inherited, with symptoms usually appearing in the 50s or 60s.
Glaucoma is a condition caused by optic nerve damage related to high pressure in the fluid circulating in the front of the eye, and is a leading cause of blindness in the United States.
If halos or colored rings appear suddenly around lights, it could be a sign of acute angle-closure glaucoma, which is considered a medical emergency.
Keratoconus occurs when the cornea progressively thins and causes a cone-like bulge; the cause of keratoconus isn't known.
Photokeratitis, or sunburned eyes, results from too much ultraviolet (UV) light and usually goes away on its own within a day or two.
Halos caused by LASIK surgery usually only last for a few weeks after the surgery.
An ocular migraine is a rare type of migraine that causes visual disturbances, including flashing or shimmering lights, zigzagging lines, and halos.
Halos from wearing glasses or contact lenses can occur when looking at a bright light source, and researchers are working on lenses that minimize this effect.
When the eye's surface is too dry, light entering the eye can scatter and cause halos, especially at night.

Prevention tips include protecting eyes from UV radiation, controlling blood sugar if diabetic, eating foods rich in vitamin C, vitamin A, and carotenoids, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding excess alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Regular eye examinations are recommended especially after turning 40 to help prevent eye disorders that cause halos.
The article was medically reviewed by Ann Marie Griff, O.D. and written by Jacquelyn Cafasso, with a current version dated May 23, 2019.
